title: The Case of the Upside-Down Fountain
label: A Bizzing mystery
setting: the Story Garden, the Fable Fountain

officeObject.name: a stone frog
officeObject.art: carved by Juniper's grandad, from the edge of the old frog hollow: a small mossy stone frog with a carved smile, about the size of a child's fist.

arc.beat: CLOCK vanishes from the fountain plaque ("When the garden ____ strikes eight, the gates close…"); a waxed calling card floats in the basin
Silas Crane's first PUBLIC NOTICE: the headline says the fountain will be "improved"; the fine print says the Story Garden will close, and reopen by ticket
Act I beat: Crane arrives in person, smiling, with a silver pen (at the gate, in the reveal)

Seed for Case 11 (scene detail, not a document): on the bandstand table behind the Committee lies their guest book, open. Its last entry, set in live text the child can zoom into, reads "Tuesday, 6 p.m. — Mrs Olive Dean, visiting puzzle-setter". In the same painting a tall woman with a long grey plait, a green coat and a violin case is walking out of frame. Nobody remarks on her, and she is never a suspect.

sceneDetail.where: the bandstand table behind the Committee, in the DOC 3.1 scene
sceneDetail.liveText: Tuesday, 6 p.m. — Mrs Olive Dean, visiting puzzle-setter

arc.beat: Eerie seeds for Case 11 (they never name her): the waxed card is bone dry after a night afloat and smells of violets; Tam hears a fiddle in the fog on Tuesday night; Juniper thanks the agency for a tune nobody played.
Nell's thread: that night, Nell takes the Inspector application out of her basket, smooths it flat, writes her name in the first box, and puts it back. Not yet.

card.text:
Every morning, the Fable Fountain runs backwards, up into the stone fox's mouth.
All night the garden is locked, and only the keeper has a key.
The Committee calls it a curse.
At noon, they sign a stranger's offer to fix it.
Then the garden may never be free again.
Read closely, detective.
Curses do not leave footprints.

cutscene.place: The Story Garden, Wednesday, seven in the morning.
cutscene.picture: Thick white mist on the hedges. Somewhere inside it, the bandstand clock ticks, slow and loud. The Fable Fountain: a stone fox sitting on a rock, mouth open. Water should pour *out* of the fox's mouth into the basin. Instead the basin is half empty, and the water is gurgling *up* and *into* the fox's mouth with a long, wet, sucking sound, like a fox drinking through a straw. The fox's stone eyes shine wet.

lines.direction: keys in one hand, the gate still swinging

cutscene.picture: A note arrives by dumbwaiter, under a cinnamon bun. Felix reads it.

lines.text: 'Come at once. The fountain is cursed. We sign Mr Crane's offer at noon. Yours, Constance Bellamy, Chair.' Footnote: *cursed* is an old word. Footnote to the footnote: so is *Constance*.

cutscene.picture: Nell is already on The Comet.

lines.text: A committee that wants money says *curse*. I smell a plan. Hunch-o-meter: ten!
You smell a cinnamon bun. Bring me facts. Before noon.

cutscene.picture: Asha and Dev run behind, into the mist.

lines.text: My turn to carry the torch.

cutscene.picture: On every lamppost on the way, the same crisp cream notice with a gold border. Its bottom strip of print is too small to read from the path.

lines.text: Seven fifty-two. Four hours and eight minutes to noon.
Half a bun. You dropped half in the mist.

cast.name: Mr Ambrose Grail
cast.look: Broad, grey whiskers, enormous boots, a ring of keys on his belt the size of a dinner plate
cast.manner: Gruff and fair; grumbles about midges; secretly feeds the robins
cast.motive: Sick of being bossed by the Committee, and of the "midge hotel"; a cursed fountain gets ripped out, hollow and all
cast.secret: He is afraid of the garden in the dark. Since the "joker" began he comes back at ten and sits all night in his hut with the lamp turned up, never once past the door

cast.name: Juniper Thorne
cast.look: Short curly hair, green frog-pattern wellies, a jam jar, binoculars round her neck
cast.manner: Quiet, earnest, careful with words; never tells a lie, but sometimes doesn't answer
cast.motive: Her frogs' pond is drying up in the drought
cast.secret: She is frightened of gruff Mr Grail, who wrote that the hollow should be filled with soil, so she never dared ask him

cast.name: Mrs Constance Bellamy
cast.note: Chair of the Fountain Restoration Committee (speaks for the Committee)
cast.look: Large hat with silk flowers, a clipboard, reading glasses on a chain she never uses
cast.manner: Dramatic; calls everyone "darling"; loves the word *cursed*
cast.motive: A "curse" brings Mr Crane's money and a grand restoration, with the Committee's name on a new plaque
cast.secret: She cannot read small print without the glasses she is too proud to wear, so she never read Crane's notice

cast.name: Mr Haris Qadir
cast.look: Overalls, a pencil behind each ear, a spirit level in his pocket
cast.manner: Says "fact" a lot; very calm; enjoys a pipe more than most people enjoy cake

cast.name: Tam Bellweather
cast.look: Flour on her sleeve, a comma whistle round her neck (since Case 2)
cast.manner: In a hurry; her notes still have no full stops

cast.name: Constable Bram Tully
cast.look: Cocoa flask, a lead with no dog on it
cast.manner: "I've brought the keys. Oh, Mr Grail has the keys."

cast.name: Silas Crane
cast.look: Long grey coat, a silver tape measure, a silver pen, a stack of crisp notices
cast.manner: Smiling, smooth, pleasant to everyone; never raises his voice

docs.title: The Fountain Report
docs.author: Mrs Constance Bellamy, for the Fountain Restoration Committee
docs.where: handed to the agency at the fountain, on lilac paper
docs.picture: a lilac report in a ribbon folder, a pressed rose clipped to the corner.
docs.body:
THE FOUNTAIN REPORT
For five mornings, the water has run backwards, into the fox's mouth.
[[c:cursed|The fountain was cursed]] by an unhappy spirit.
[[c:everyone|Everyone agrees.]]
[[c:saddest|It is the saddest sight in all of Inkwell.]]
Only a full restoration will lift the curse.
Happily, a kind gentleman has offered to pay. (See his notice.)
Our meeting closed [[c:committee-seven|at seven o'clock]], and we all went home together.
— C. Bellamy, Chair

docs.title: Engineer's log
docs.author: Mr Haris Qadir, water engineer
docs.when: Tuesday, half past seven in the morning
docs.where: his clipboard, hanging on the valve box
docs.picture: a squared engineer's log sheet on a clipboard, a neat sketch of a lever with two positions, A and B.
docs.body:
ENGINEER'S LOG — Fable Fountain
Tuesday. Half past seven, morning.
Pump fine. No damage.
[[c:posB|Valve found in position B.]]
Position A pushes water up and out of the fox.
Position B is called "fill". It pulls water back through the fox.
[[c:fill-hollow|It sends it down the old pipe to the hollow behind the yew hedge.]]
[[c:prints|Small boot prints by the valve box. Wavy soles.]]
Valve box latch: stiff, but not locked.

docs.title: Keeper's log
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail, park keeper
docs.where: the keeper's hut, hanging on a nail
docs.picture: a battered ruled logbook with a muddy thumbprint and a pencil on a string.
docs.body:
KEEPER'S LOG — A. Grail
Every evening this week:
[[c:grail-eight|8 p.m. Valve in A. Gates locked.]] Home for tea.
Every morning this week:
7 a.m. Gates unlocked. [[c:grail-seven|Valve in B again!]] Put it back to A.
Note to self: no rain for three weeks.
Note to self: who is having a laugh at me?
Note to self: midges. [[c:grail-soil|That old hollow should be filled with soil.]]

docs.title: Help the Frogs!
docs.author: Juniper Thorne
docs.where: pinned to the Story Garden noticeboard, beside the bandstand, two weeks ago (the felt pen has faded a little in the sun)
docs.picture: a home-made poster in felt pen: a drawing of three cross-eyed, very worried frogs and one cracked, dry pond. In the bottom corner, very small, a drawing of a little arched door.
docs.body:
HELP THE FROGS!
The hollow behind the yew hedge is a frog pond.
Well, it was.
[[c:dust|Now my frogs are dry as dust.]]
[[c:grandad|Grandad Thorne kept this garden once. He says the fox used to feed the frogs.]]
Please, somebody, help them.
— Juniper Thorne, age 9
Garden Cottage ([[c:green-door|the house with the green door in the wall]])

hiddenClue.note: The clue hidden in plain sight. The address at the bottom of a child's poster looks like the least important line on the desk. It answers the impossible question: the locked garden has a door that is not a gate. The reveal comes back to it: "It was on the very first page."

docs.title: The fountain plaque, with a calling card
docs.author: the fountain's builder, long ago (the card: unknown)
docs.where: on the fountain's stone rim; the card floating in the basin
docs.picture: a weathered bronze plaque on the fountain rim (lettering is live text, not painted). On the water floats a small waxed card with one perfect round ink blot.
docs.body:
THE FABLE FOUNTAIN
Here the thirsty fox gives back the water the river gave him.
[[c:plaque|When the garden ____ strikes eight, the gates close and the fox sleeps.]]
One word is missing. The gap is neat and clean.
Floating in the basin is a small waxed card.
It has a perfect ink blot. The ink has not run.
[[c:card|Look below the surface.]] Read on forthwith. — B.

docs.title: Public Notice
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: pinned to the Story Garden gate, and to every lamppost on the way there
docs.picture: a crisp cream notice with a gold border, a grand headline space at the top, and a strip of tiny print at the very bottom that you have to lean in to read.
docs.body:
PUBLIC NOTICE
[[c:improved|GOOD NEWS! THE FABLE FOUNTAIN WILL BE IMPROVED!]]
Kindly paid for by Crane Holdings.
A brighter, better Story Garden for everyone!
With warm wishes, Silas Crane

[[c:fineprint|During the improvement works, the Story Garden will close to the public.]]
[[c:until|It will close from 1 November until further notice.]]
[[c:tickets|Afterwards, entry will be by ticket only.]]

finePrint.note: The fine print is set in the app's smallest legible size; the magnifier enlarges it like anything else. It is an arc clue, never needed to solve the case, and the reveal reads it aloud.

docs.title: Mr Ambrose Grail: When do you check the valve?
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail
docs.body:
Twice a day, regular as rain. Well, when we had rain.
At eight every evening I check it's in A, and I lock the gates.
At seven every morning I unlock them.
And every morning this week it's in B.
[[c:leg|Somebody's pulling my leg.]]

docs.title: Mr Ambrose Grail: Who has keys to the gates?
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail
docs.body:
Me. Only me.
[[c:keys|The keys never leave my belt, not even in the bath.]]
Don't ask how I know that's true. It is.

docs.title: Mr Ambrose Grail: What do you think of the hollow behind the yew hedge?
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail
docs.body:
A midge hotel, that's what.
I'd fill it with soil tomorrow if the Committee let me.
[[c:grail-why|Why would I send water there? I'd be feeding the midges.]]

docs.title: Mr Ambrose Grail: What boots do you wear?
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail
docs.body:
Size twelve. Same pair for twenty years.
[[c:grail-boots|The soles are as flat as a pancake.]]
I don't slip, mind. I just stomp.

docs.title: Mr Ambrose Grail: Where do you go after you lock up?
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail
docs.body:
Home for my tea, in Mill Lane, outside the garden.
A kipper and a crossword.
I'm in my slippers by quarter past eight. Ask the robins.

docs.title: Mr Ambrose Grail: Why is there a camp bed in your hut?
docs.author: Mr Ambrose Grail
docs.body:
*(He turns his cap round and round.)*
[[c:grail-back|Since the joker started, I come back at ten.]]
I sit in the hut with the lamp turned up, all night.
I mean to catch him. I never do.
[[c:grail-hut|I never go past the hut door. Not in the dark.]]
The garden's different at night. It whispers.
Don't tell the robins.

docs.title: Juniper Thorne: Where do you live?
docs.author: Juniper Thorne
docs.body:
Garden Cottage, next to the Story Garden.
[[c:juniper-door|Our green door opens right into the garden, by the yew hedge.]]
Mum says it's the best door in Inkwell.

docs.title: Juniper Thorne: What do you wear in the garden?
docs.author: Juniper Thorne
docs.body:
[[c:wellies|My frog wellies. They have wavy soles, like ripples.]]
Frogs like ripples.
Well, they like ripples in water. These are rubber.

docs.title: Juniper Thorne: When do you visit your frogs?
docs.author: Juniper Thorne
docs.body:
Every evening.
[[c:after-bell|After the garden clock strikes eight, I say goodnight to them.]]
Then I go in for my bath.
They have a bath too, now.

docs.title: Juniper Thorne: Who told you about the fountain?
docs.author: Juniper Thorne
docs.body:
Grandad. He was the keeper here before Mr Grail.
He drew a map of every pipe in this garden.
[[c:grandad-showed|He showed me the fox's secret when I was six.]]
I wasn't supposed to tell anyone. So I didn't.

docs.title: Juniper Thorne: Are your frogs really dry as dust?
docs.author: Juniper Thorne
docs.body:
Well, no. Frogs can't be dust. That's just a saying.
It means the hollow was drying up.
[[c:full-again|But now it's full again every morning.]]
They're very happy. They sing.

docs.title: Mrs Constance Bellamy: Why do you say the fountain was cursed?
docs.author: Mrs Constance Bellamy
docs.body:
Because it's spooky, darling!
[[c:spooky|Water going backwards is simply spooky.]]
And Mr Crane says a curse is very bad for a garden.
He has offered to fix everything. Such a kind man.
We sign his offer at noon.

docs.title: Mrs Constance Bellamy: Where did the Committee go after your meeting?
docs.author: Mrs Constance Bellamy
docs.body:
We closed at seven and walked out of the gates together.
[[c:gates-open|The gates were still open then, of course.]]
I was home by half past, having cocoa with my cat, Sir Reginald.

docs.title: Mrs Constance Bellamy: Have you looked at the valve?
docs.author: Mrs Constance Bellamy
docs.body:
The what? Darling, I don't do valves.
I do committees.
[[c:no-valve|I've never even seen the valve box.]]

docs.title: Mrs Constance Bellamy: Who wrote the public notice?
docs.author: Mrs Constance Bellamy
docs.body:
Mr Crane himself! Such a smile.
He gave us a hundred copies.
*(Her reading glasses swing on their chain. She does not put them on.)*
[[c:small-bits|I haven't read the small bits. Nobody reads the small bits.]]

docs.title: Mr Haris Qadir: Can a curse turn a valve?
docs.author: Mr Haris Qadir
docs.body:
In my experience, curses do not have hands.
A valve needs a hand.
It needs someone who knows which way to push it.
[[c:knew-pipe|Whoever did this knew the old pipe was there.]]

docs.title: Mr Haris Qadir: Who knows about the old pipe?
docs.author: Mr Haris Qadir
docs.body:
It isn't on the new plans.
[[c:old-map|Only the old keeper's map shows it.]]
Keeper Thorne drew that map, forty years ago. Lovely pipes.

docs.title: Tam's sighting note
docs.author: Tam Bellweather
docs.body:
8 oclock garden wall lamps lit
[[c:tam-torch|saw a little torch by the yew hedge after the gates shut]]
frog noises
it went back in the green door
later [[c:tam-fiddle|a fiddle somwhere in the fog]]. sad tune. then nothing
tam

aside.text: Tam skids in through the gate with a bun in one hand and a note in the other. It is about last night, Tuesday. Tam hands over a note, written in a hurry.
Footnote: *it* means the torch. Footnote to the footnote: torches do not open doors. Someone was holding it.
And Mr Grail lives in Mill Lane. There's no green door in Mill Lane.

questions.portrait: nervous: she has said a little too much

questions.q: Who told you about the fountain?
Are your frogs really dry as dust?
questions.portrait: guilty → relieved. When Mr Grail stomps past the bandstand, she steps behind Asha and says nothing at all.

questions.q: Why do you say the fountain was cursed?
Where did the Committee go after your meeting?
Have you looked at the valve?

questions.portrait: calm → nervous, much later, in the reveal

questions.q: Can a curse turn a valve?
Who knows about the old pipe?
Did the Lamplighters see anything by the garden?

deductions.statement: "The fountain was cursed" is only an opinion: nobody saw a curse. The fact is that somebody moves the valve to B in the night.
deductions.why: a sentence can *sound* like a fact ("was cursed", "Everyone agrees") and still be an opinion. A fact can be checked: the valve was in position B, and Mr Grail found it there every morning. Facts point to a *hand*, not a curse.

deductions.statement: "Dry as dust" does not mean the frogs are dust. It means their pond was drying up. Position B sends water to that very pond. Whoever moved the valve wanted to fill the frogs' hollow.
deductions.why: the figure of speech hides a real worry. And "the fox used to feed the frogs" is figurative too, but it points at something literal: the old pipe from the fox to the hollow, which only Keeper Thorne's family knew.

deductions.statement: The valve was in A at eight, when the gates were locked, and in B by seven next morning. So it was moved after the gates shut, by someone who did not need the gate: someone with a door straight into the garden, wearing wavy-soled boots.
deductions.why: this is the **timeline join**. Two documents by two different people (the keeper's log and Juniper's own answer) fit together at *eight o'clock*. Before eight: valve in A, gates open. After eight: gates locked, and Juniper is in the garden through her green door. It is also the answer to the impossible question: a locked garden is only locked to people who need the gate.

deductions.statement: The vanished word: the plaque's gap is in the same place as Juniper's words "the garden clock strikes eight". The missing word is CLOCK.
deductions.why: Arc clue: optional mark, logged in the back of the notebook.

deductions.statement: Crane's notice: the headline says *improved*; the small print says *closed*, then *tickets*. Confirmed by "nobody reads the small bits", which is exactly what the notice counts on.
deductions.why: Arc clue: optional mark, logged in the back of the notebook.

arcMarks.note: The Blot's card: "Look below the surface", the advice for the whole case (and, though nobody knows it yet, the whole season).
The fiddle in the fog: nobody in the case owns a fiddle. Logged under *Blot?* with a question mark.

wrongLinks.quill: Is anybody really pulling his leg? Show me the leg.
One of these can be checked. One is a feeling. Which is which?
A man who won't walk past his own hut door in the dark. Would he cross the whole garden to the yew hedge?

redHerrings.note: Mr Grail has the only keys, says somebody is "pulling my leg", and someone slept in his hut. He wants the hollow *filled with soil*, the opposite of filling it with water; his soles are flat, and the prints have wavy soles. In Chapter 4 the torch is seen going home through the green door (he lives in Mill Lane), and he admits he never goes past the hut door in the dark. *Pulling my leg* is figurative: he means someone is teasing him.

The Committee has a reason to want a "curse": a kind gentleman will pay. They left at seven, while the gates were open; at eight the valve was still in A. Their report is opinion, but an opinion is not a crime.

timeline.to: half past seven the next morning

events.text: The Committee's meeting closes; they walk out of the open gates together
Mr Grail checks the valve: A. He locks the gates and goes home for tea
The garden clock strikes eight; Juniper comes out through the green door to say goodnight to her frogs
Tam lights the garden-wall lamps and sees a little torch by the yew hedge, which goes back in the green door
Mr Grail comes back and sits in his hut with the lamp up, never past the door
All night, the fountain runs "backwards" and the hollow fills
events.note: no time word: the child infers it from 2 and 7

events.text: Mr Grail unlocks the gates and finds the valve in B
Mr Qadir logs position B and small, wavy boot prints

shake.quill: Could they walk out of *open* gates after they were *locked*?

wrongSuspect.grail: Read the last note in his log. Would a man who wants the hollow filled with soil fill it with water? Now look at his boots.
wrongSuspect.bellamy: When did they go home? And when was the valve last seen in A?

accusation.weakEvidence: You have shown that someone moved the valve. Who could be in the garden after eight, when the gates were locked? And who *wanted* that hollow full?
accusation.note: Juniper Thorne, who has been switching the valve to "fill" every evening after the gates close, to save her frogs' pond in the drought.

wrongTheory.curse: Curses do not have hands. Find me the hand.

revealSetting: The fountain, a quarter to eleven. The mist has burnt off and the stone fox is still drinking. Everyone is here: Mr Grail on the bench with his cap in his hands, Mrs Bellamy with her clipboard and a silver pen of her own, Mr Qadir with a spanner, Juniper with her jam jar, Tam with a bun, the agency, and Constable Tully with a lead and no dog. The bandstand clock ticks.

reveal.text: New detective. Fifteen minutes. Was the fountain cursed?
No. The report says, "The fountain was cursed." That's an opinion. The engineer's log says, "Valve found in position B." That's a fact.
But *everyone agrees*, darling!
Footnote: "everyone agrees" is not evidence. Footnote to the footnote: I didn't agree. Nobody asked me.
Then whose hand moved the valve? In a locked garden, with one ring of keys?
I said Mr Grail. *(She winces.)* It was a ten.
The hut's mine. Lamp up, door shut, all night. I don't like the garden in the dark.
But the garden has a door that isn't a gate. It was on the very first page: "the house with the green door in the wall."
On Juniper's poster. We all read it. Nobody saw it.
Valve in A at eight, gates locked. After the clock struck eight, Juniper went out to her frogs. Tam saw the torch go home through the green door.
And the boot prints have wavy soles. Like ripples. *(quietly)* Hunch-o-meter: seven.
Juniper. Will you tell us why?
The frogs were dry as dust. Grandad showed me the fox's secret. Lever to B, and the fox feeds the frogs. So every evening, I pushed it.
And every morning I pushed it back.
I'm sorry, Mr Grail. I didn't ask, because you wrote you'd fill it with soil. I was scared of you.
…And I'm scared of the dark. Seems we're square, girl.
Fact: the pump is fine. Fact: the frogs are in excellent voice.
Mrs Bellamy, before you sign, may I read you the small bits?
Nell reads the fine print aloud through the magnifier. Mrs Bellamy's glasses, for the first time ever, go on her nose.
I never could read small print without these. Too proud. *Close* the garden? *Tickets*? For *frogs*? The Committee withdraws its thanks!
At the gate, a man in a long grey coat puts away his silver pen, and smiles.
Everyone reads the headline, Miss Okafor-Hart. That is rather the point of headlines. Good morning.
He tips his hat and walks away, still smiling. The bandstand clock strikes eleven.
Thank you for the fiddle last night. The frogs loved it.
What fiddle?
Somebody played a sad tune over the wall. Wasn't it you?
Nobody answers. A robin sings. In Dev's pocket, the dry waxed card smells, very faintly, of violets.

epilogue.text: A pond for the frogs.

By Saturday the whole town is digging. Mr Grail brings the biggest spade ("Midges and all, then"). Mr Qadir fits a rain barrel and a little trickle-pipe, so the hollow fills from the bandstand roof whenever it rains, and the fountain runs forwards for good. Bellweather's Bakery sends buns. Tam blows the comma whistle at every pause in Mr Grail's speech, which is a lot of pauses. Juniper names the biggest frog **Grail**. Mr Grail pretends not to be pleased. Juniper gives him her second-best torch, "for the dark bits". He keeps it on his belt, next to the keys.
The Committee

holds a bake sale to restore the fountain itself. They raise enough, and a bit more. Mrs Bellamy now wears her glasses on her nose, and reads everything, including the backs of seed packets. Her new report says: "The fountain was cursed. *(Opinion.)* It is now fixed. *(Fact.)*" Felix frames a copy.
The vanished word.
Dev reads the plaque again with Juniper's answer beside it.
"When the garden ____ strikes eight." What strikes? A clock does.
The garden *clock*! On the bandstand. Grandad wound it every Sunday.
The new detective writes **CLOCK** into the Blot Ledger. The ink spreads: **UNDER · THE · CLOCK**.
Three words, three cases. Breakfast, three minutes. That's probably nothing.
Probably. *(He frowns at the Ledger. Then a cinnamon bun arrives, and he stops frowning.)*
The card said "Look below the surface." Footnote: so did the engineer. Footnote to the footnote: so did the frogs, I expect.
Biscuit.

Constable Tully finds Biscuit at last, asleep on the *roof* of the bandstand, right under the garden clock. Nobody can work out how he got up there. Mr Grail fetches a ladder. Biscuit comes down only for a bun.
The office object.
Juniper climbs all 39 stairs with something heavy in her jam jar: a little stone frog, mossy and smiling, that sat at the edge of the old hollow.
Grandad carved it. He says it's been watching the pond for forty years. It can watch your shelf now.
Thank you, Juniper. It has good eyes.
The **stone frog** goes on the shelf, beside the lamplighter's hook. When you tap it, it gives one small, satisfied *croak*.
Nell's thread.
That night, Nell takes the Inspector application out of her basket, smooths it flat, writes her name in the first box, and puts it back. Not yet.

drill.title: Fact or Opinion?
drill.subtitle: with a figurative bonus
drill.intro: Clue Spotter, sorting edition. Six lines from the case slide onto the desk, one at a time. The child sorts each into the FACT drawer (it can be checked) or the OPINION drawer (it is what someone thinks or feels).

items.quill: Could you go and look? Yes.

items.prompt: "8 p.m. Valve in A. Gates locked."
items.quill: Written at the time, by the person who did it.

items.prompt: "It is the saddest sight in all of Inkwell."
"Small boot prints by the valve box. Wavy soles."

bonus.title: Figurative bonus
bonus.intro: For each saying, the child taps the picture that shows what it *really* means, and laughs at the picture that shows it *literally*.

backgrounds: The Story Garden at dawn: thick white mist on clipped hedges, the bandstand with a round clock face (hands painted, no numerals) half lost in the mist, dew on the grass, a robin on the gate. Warm greens, soft gold light breaking through. Spooky-soft, never frightening: the kind of mist you want to walk into with a torch and a friend.

The Fable Fountain, close: a stone fox sitting on a rock above a round basin, mouth open, stone eyes wet. The "backwards" morning version: basin half empty, water swirling up into the fox's mouth. A small bronze plaque on the rim (blank). A tiny waxed card afloat.
Behind the yew hedge: a mossy hollow; in the "before" plate, cracked mud with three anxious frogs; in the "after" plate, full and rippling, lily pads, frogs singing.

The green door in the wall: a small arched wooden door, painted green, set in the old brick garden wall, with Garden Cottage's chimney beyond. In the opening panels it should be visible but unremarkable, half behind ivy.
The valve box: a squat iron box half-hidden in ferns by the hedge, lid open, a lever with two notches. Small wavy boot prints in the mud.

The keeper's hut, inside (seen through Dev's periscope): a camp bed, a folded grey blanket, a flask, a lantern burnt to the bottom of its glass, a pair of enormous boots by the door. Cosy, a little sad, nothing sinister.
The garden gate at evening: iron gates, a big padlock, a lamppost with Crane's notice pinned to it (blank gold-edged sheet).

The bandstand scene behind the Committee (DOC 3.1): their guest book lies open on the bandstand table; its last entry is live text the child can zoom into ("Tuesday, 6 p.m. — Mrs Olive Dean, visiting puzzle-setter"), not painted. In the same painting a tall woman with a long grey plait, a green coat and a violin case is walking out of frame. Nobody remarks on her; she is never a suspect (seed for Case 11).

Mr Qadir's clipboard with a sketch of lever positions A and B
Juniper's felt-pen frog poster (with a tiny drawn door in one corner)
Crane's crisp notice with a gold border
a key ring the size of a dinner plate
the Committee's guest book, open (last entry in live text)
the camp bed and burnt-down lantern in the hut
portraits: Mr Grail: broad, weathered face, grey whiskers, flat cap, huge boots. Offended is a deep frown; amused is a hidden smile under the whiskers. Guilty is the cap turning in his hands. Kind underneath, always.
Juniper: nine, short curly hair, freckles, binoculars, frog wellies, jam jar. Guilty is eyes down and the jar held close, never tearful; relieved is a big, gap-toothed smile.
Mrs Bellamy: silk-flower hat, pearls, clipboard, glasses on a chain. Amused is theatrical; nervous is a hand fluttering at her pearls. A last-scene variant with the glasses on her nose.
Mr Qadir: overalls, a pencil behind each ear, a calm half-smile. Two expressions are enough.
Silas Crane: long grey coat, neat grey hair, silver tape measure, silver pen, wide smile. Amused and calm only. He should look charming, never sinister: a man who is sure he has already won.
art.notes: No lettering in any painting; plaques and notices are blank shapes, the text is live. Comic panels: opening (5 panels as scripted); reveal (6 panels: the report and the log side by side; the poster's green door circled by the magnifier; Juniper at dusk by the green door with a torch; Mr Grail and Juniper, square at last; Nell reading the fine print, Mrs Bellamy's glasses going on; Crane pocketing his pen at the gate as the clock strikes eleven). Office object: a small mossy stone frog with a carved smile, about the size of a child's fist.

exercises.prompt:
Mr Grail writes: "7 a.m. Gates unlocked."
Un- means "undo". So the gates were…
exercises.explain: Un + locked = unlocked. Un- undoes the word after it. Locked gates are shut; unlocked gates can open. Think of untie and unpack.

exercises.prompt:
"He says the fox used to feed the frogs."
Who is "He"?
exercises.explain: Look at the sentence just before. It says Grandad Thorne kept this garden once. So "He" is Grandad Thorne.

exercises.prompt: Put Mr Grail's morning in order, first to last.
options: He puts the valve back to A.
He unlocks the gates at 7 a.m.
He finds the valve in B.
answer: He unlocks the gates at 7 a.m.
He finds the valve in B.
He puts the valve back to A.
exercises.explain: His log says: "7 a.m. Gates unlocked. Valve in B again! Put it back to A." You cannot fix the valve before you find it in B.

exercises.prompt:
"The soles are as flat as a pancake."
What does Mr Grail mean?
options: His boots are made of pancake.
He eats pancakes in his boots.
exercises.explain: This is a simile. It uses "as … as" to compare two things. His soles are not pancakes. They are just very, very flat.

exercises.prompt:
Tam wrote "8 oclock".
How should "oclock" be written?
exercises.explain: O'clock is short for "of the clock". The apostrophe sits where the missing letters were. Tam's notes are quick, so she leaves it out.

exercises.prompt:
Mrs Bellamy writes: "The fountain was cursed"
The engineer writes: "Valve found in position B."
Which one is a fact you can check?
options: Both of them can be checked.
exercises.explain: A fact can be checked. Anyone can open the box and look at the valve. Nobody saw a curse, so "cursed" is only Mrs Bellamy's opinion.

exercises.prompt:
Juniper's poster says, "Now my frogs are dry as dust."
What does she mean?
options: The frogs have turned to dust.
The frogs need a dust bath.
exercises.explain: "Dry as dust" is a saying. It means very dry. The frogs are not dust. Their pond in the hollow has almost no water, and there has been no rain for three weeks.

exercises.prompt:
"It sends it down the old pipe to the hollow behind the yew hedge."
What is the hollow?
options: a tree with a hole inside
exercises.explain: Use the other documents. Juniper's poster says the hollow is a frog pond. Mr Grail wants to fill it with soil. So it is a low dip in the ground.

exercises.prompt:
Position B is called "fill". "It pulls water back through the fox."
What does "It" stand for?
exercises.explain: The sentence before is about position B. "It" picks up that idea, so position B is what pulls the water back.

exercises.prompt:
The notice shouts, "THE FABLE FOUNTAIN WILL BE IMPROVED!"
Read the small print. What will really happen to the garden?
options: It will close, and later you will need a ticket.
Everyone will get in free, every single day of the year.
It will get a brand new fox.
exercises.answer: It will close, and later you will need a ticket.
exercises.explain: The big words say "improved". The small words say the garden will close from 1 November, then open by ticket only. Always read the small print.

exercises.prompt:
Mr Grail writes: "8 p.m. Valve in A. Gates locked."
Which sentence says it best?
options: At 8 p.m., the valve was in A the gates were locked.
The gates were locked at 8 p.m. because the valve was in A.
At 8 p.m., the valve was in A and the gates were locked.
exercises.answer: At 8 p.m., the valve was in A and the gates were locked.
exercises.explain: A log uses short notes. In a full sentence, "and" joins two things that both happened. "Because" would say one caused the other, which the log never says.

exercises.prompt:
Mrs Bellamy says, "Water going backwards is simply spooky."
Which part is a fact, and which is her opinion?
options: Both parts are facts, because she is the Chair.
Backwards water is a fact; spooky is her opinion.
Both parts are opinions, because she wasn't there.
exercises.answer: Backwards water is a fact; spooky is her opinion.
exercises.explain: The engineer and the keeper both saw the water run backwards, so that part can be checked. "Spooky" is a feeling. Being the Chair does not turn a feeling into a fact.

exercises.prompt:
Mrs Bellamy writes, "The fountain was cursed by an unhappy spirit."
Rewrite it so the doer comes first. Which is right?
options: The fountain cursed an unhappy spirit.
An unhappy spirit cursed the fountain.
An unhappy spirit was cursed by the fountain.
exercises.answer: An unhappy spirit cursed the fountain.
exercises.explain: This is the passive voice: the thing acted on comes first. The active voice puts the doer first. Said plainly, it is easier to ask: did anybody see a spirit do it?

exercises.prompt:
Asked about the hollow, Mr Grail says, "A midge hotel, that's what."
What kind of language is this?
exercises.explain: A metaphor says one thing IS another, with no "like" or "as". The hollow is not a hotel, but midges crowd there as if they had booked rooms.

exercises.prompt:
The notice says, "During the improvement works, the Story Garden will close to the public."
Improve + -ment makes "improvement". What does -ment do?
options: turns a verb into a noun
exercises.answer: turns a verb into a noun
exercises.explain: Improve is a doing word (a verb). Add -ment and you get improvement, a thing (a noun). The same works for move, movement and pay, payment.

exercises.prompt:
The poster says, "The hollow behind the yew hedge is a frog pond. Well, it was."
Why does it switch from "is" to "was"?
options: It was a pond, but it has dried up.
It will be a pond next year.
She wrote in a hurry and mixed her verbs up, so both should say "is".
exercises.answer: It was a pond, but it has dried up.
exercises.explain: The present tense "is" says what it should be now. Then "Well, it was" corrects it with the past tense: it used to be a pond. The change of tense tells you the pond has dried.

exercises.prompt:
Mrs Bellamy says, "Nobody reads the small bits."
Why might Mr Crane put the closing of the garden in small print?
options: The printer ran out of ink for big letters halfway down the page.
Small print is the easiest kind to read.
He hopes people see the good news and miss the closing.
exercises.answer: He hopes people see the good news and miss the closing.
exercises.explain: Big cheerful words grab your eye; small words hide. If nobody reads the small bits, nobody notices the garden will close and need tickets.

exercises.prompt:
Juniper says Grandad "showed me the fox's secret when I was six."
The engineer says only the old keeper's map shows the old pipe. What was the fox's secret?
options: a spare key to the gates, hidden under the stone fox's paw
that position B sends water down the old pipe to the hollow
a way to make the fox drink
exercises.answer: that position B sends water down the old pipe to the hollow
exercises.explain: Grandad Thorne drew the only map of the old pipe. He showed Juniper the secret, so she knew which way to push the valve to fill her frogs' pond.

boardIntro.text: Forget the Committee. Look. The garden is locked all night.
One ring of keys, and it never leaves his belt. Not even in the bath.
And somebody slept in that hut.

aside.text: The Story Garden, a little before eight. The mist has not lifted. The bandstand clock ticks somewhere inside it, and the fountain gives a long, slurping gulp every few seconds, as if the fox is very thirsty and slightly rude. Robins hop on the padlocked side gate. Behind the yew hedge, where no rain has fallen for three weeks, the air smells of wet moss.
Dev fishes the waxed card out of the basin with a twig. It has been floating all night, and it is bone dry. He sniffs it.
Nobody in the garden is wearing violets. And from behind the yew hedge, where no rain has fallen for three weeks, comes the sound of a very happy frog.
The interviews happen on the bandstand steps. The mist is thinning into gold. Every few seconds the fountain gulps.
Dev puts his biscuit-tin periscope to the dusty window of the keeper's hut. Somewhere in the mist, the bandstand clock ticks on.

lines.text: There's a camp bed in there. And a blanket. And a lamp burnt right down to the bottom.
He said he was home in his slippers.

aside.text: Constable Tully puffs up the path, cocoa slopping. At the hut door, Mr Grail has heard every word. He takes off his cap, turns it round and round in his big hands, and says nothing at all.

lines.text: He says he was home in his slippers. But someone spent the night in that hut.
A locked garden. One ring of keys. One man inside it all night. Hunch-o-meter: *ten*.
He could change his boots. He has had twenty years to buy another pair.
Message from Mrs Bellamy. Mr Crane has a train at noon. They're signing at *eleven* now.

aside.text: The bandstand clock says twenty to eleven. Through the bars of the gate, the children see a long grey coat, and the glint of a silver pen being uncapped.
